passage:
I was the fourth employee at the startup, so I sat two desks from Varun and saw more than he probably realised. My name is Mansi.

On a Monday in June, the bank balance on the shared dashboard showed a figure that made everyone go quiet. Varun looked at it for a long time, rubbed his eyes and closed the laptop. At lunch he barely ate.

On Wednesday he called the whole team into the meeting room, along with his co-founder, Nitin. "We have about ten weeks of cash," he said. "I should have told you sooner. I'm going to talk to the investors this week, and whatever happens, salaries and notice come first."

Nitin added that they'd help everyone with references.

I can't tell what Varun felt. His hands were tight on the table. But nobody left the room feeling lied to.

qa.q: How many weeks of cash did Varun say the startup had?
qa.a: Varun said they had about ten weeks of cash.

qa.q: What might Varun have been feeling when he closed the laptop, and how sure can Mansi be?
qa.a: Varun seemed weighed down and responsible, since he went quiet and barely ate, but Mansi says his inner state cannot be known for certain.

qa.q: What would you advise Varun to do after telling the team?
qa.a: Varun could talk to the investors as promised, plan an orderly wind-down or pivot, and keep protecting salaries, notice and references for the staff.

qa.q: How might the employees have felt hearing the news directly?
qa.a: They may have felt worried about their jobs, but hearing the truth early from the founders probably let them feel respected rather than misled.

grounding: A co-founder feels responsible as cash runs out, tells the team the truth early and puts employees first; an employee observes it.

passage:
"Ojas, we have seven weeks of cash."
"I know, Jahnavi. I've been staring at the same spreadsheet."
"I keep thinking about Deepa and Faiz. They left good jobs for us."
"Me too. I can't sleep."
"We have to tell them. And the investors. This week."
"What if we say a new round is coming? Buy some time?"
"There isn't a round. If we say that, they stay and don't look for jobs. That's worse."
Ojas rubbed his face. "Okay. So what do we actually say?"
"The truth. Cash lasts seven weeks. We're trying one pivot for four weeks. If it doesn't work, we wind down properly. Salaries and dues get paid first, before anything else."
"And references. I'll write every single one myself."
"Monday, then. All-hands at ten."
"I feel sick about it."
"So do I. But I'd feel sicker hiding it."

qa.q: How many weeks of cash did the startup have?
What were Jahnavi and Ojas feeling about the team?
qa.a: They felt guilty and anxious, losing sleep because Deepa and Faiz had left good jobs to join them.

qa.q: What plan did Jahnavi propose instead of overpromising?
qa.a: Telling the team and investors the truth this week, trying one pivot for four weeks, then winding down properly with salaries and dues paid first.

qa.q: How might Deepa and Faiz be affected if the founders hid the numbers?
qa.a: They might stay without looking for other jobs and feel betrayed later, so the early truth protects them.

grounding: Co-founders running out of cash feel responsible for the team; they choose to tell the truth early, plan a pivot or orderly wind-down, and protect employees first.

passage:
I'm Yamini, and last year our ed-tech startup ran out of money. Ramesh and I founded it in a one-room office in Jaipur, and by the end there were nine of us. When I saw we had two months left, my first thought was to hide it. Maybe a miracle would come. I told the team, "Everything's fine," for three weeks. Every time I said it, I felt sicker.
Then Priyanka from design asked me directly if her salary was safe. I couldn't lie to her face.
That evening Ramesh and I wrote down the real numbers. On Monday, we told everyone. We told the investors the same day. We promised salaries would be paid to the last day before any other bill, and we kept that. We wrote references, made calls, and helped four people find jobs before we closed.
Looking back, the three weeks of "everything's fine" were the part I regret.

qa.q: How many people were working at the startup by the end?
How did Yamini feel while saying "Everything's fine" for three weeks?
qa.a: Yamini felt guilty and sick, knowing the company had only two months of money left.

qa.q: What did Yamini and Ramesh do once they stopped hiding it?
qa.a: They wrote down the real numbers, told the team and investors the same day, paid salaries first, and helped people find new jobs.

qa.q: How might Priyanka have felt when she asked about her salary?
qa.a: Priyanka was probably anxious and uncertain, sensing something was wrong, and needed an honest answer to plan her life.

grounding: A co-founder feels responsible as cash runs out, regrets delaying the truth, then tells the team and investors, pays employees first and winds down properly.
